_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: By inference that the first tanna holds, etc.: [this is said] in astonishment.
rashi:a4.1: And it killed him: the ox killed the digger.
rashi:a4.2: Exempt: the owner of the ox.
rashi:a4.3: Are liable to pay: evidently a loan written in the Torah is considered like one written in a document. And this is difficult for the one who established the dispute of Rabbi Yosei and the first tanna of the mishna [on 6b] as concerning where he caused damage, since if so, an anonymous ruling contradicts an anonymous ruling. And there are those who raise this objection against Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar; but it is a wonder in my eyes how one can raise it, since Rabbi Shimon is a tanna and may disagree.
rashi:a5.1: When he stood trial: before he died, and they obligated him to pay. Therefore one collects from the heirs, since once his judgment to pay has been decided, it is like a loan with a document.
rashi:a6.1: But doesn’t Ḥagga teach: died and buried him: [i.e., the ox buried him] in the pit, for example, it knocked down a section [of earth] with it; and even so the heirs are liable. [Rashi’s heading reads “But doesn’t Ḥagga teach,” without “Rav Naḥman says.”]
rashi:a6.2: And the halakha: that which it teaches, that the heirs are liable, is for example where the judges sat at the opening of the pit and obligated him to pay at once.
rashi:a7.1: They sprinkle for him: they sprinkle on his behalf the blood of his sin offering and his guilt offering; and it is not like a sin offering whose owner has died, as long as he has not been executed.
rashi:a7.2: Sinned: unwittingly, at the time that he went out to be executed; for example, he saw forbidden fat and thought it was permitted fat, and ate it.
rashi:a7.3: One does not attend to him: [to wait] for him to set aside an offering to be sacrificed.
rashi:a7.4: Because one does not afflict his judgment: [by] waiting to execute him until they slaughter the offering and the blood is sprinkled, for that is affliction of judgment.
rashi:a8.1: The first clause as well: which teaches that where he sinned before that, they sprinkle for him; there they do wait for him until it is slaughtered and [the blood] sprinkled.
rashi:a11.1: Mishna: One does not wait for her until she gives birth: rather, one executes her offspring with her, since it is one body.
rashi:a11.2: Sat on the travailing chair: before her sentence was concluded.
rashi:a11.3: One waits for her until she gives birth: since once it has uprooted and moved from its place, it is another body.
rashi:a11.4: One may derive benefit from her hair: and the Gemara explains the reason.
rashi:a11.5: Is forbidden for benefit: as we maintain (Pesaḥim 22b) [from] “And the owner of the ox shall be clear” [Exodus 21:28], like a person who says to his fellow: So-and-so has gone out clear of his property, and has no benefit of any kind from it.
rashi:a13.1: Gemara: To include the offspring: it was assumed that he derives it from “both of them,” since it could have written “and they shall die,” and I would know that “and they shall die” means no fewer than two.
rashi:a13.2: “Both of them” is superfluous, [and therefore available] for exposition.
rashi:a14.1: Both of them equal: the adulterer and the adulteress must both be subject to punishment. But if she was a minor and he an adult, or he a minor, who is not subject to punishment, and she an adult and subject to punishment, the adult is not executed. And the Gemara answers: we derive [the fetus] from “also.”
rashi:a16.1: Disgrace: for if there is life in the offspring, it will come out after its mother’s death, and that is a disgrace.
rashi:a17.1: Inherits: if an inheritance fell to him on that day, and he died that same day, he bequeaths it to his relatives on his father’s side.
rashi:a17.2: And Rav Sheshet said: this “inherits and bequeaths” cannot be explained as referring to his father’s property, since even had he not been born, his relatives would inherit his father’s property, where there are no sons [so his inheriting would change nothing].
rashi:a17.3: Rather, he inherits his mother’s property: if she died on that day; and even if he died on that day, he inherits his mother’s property and passes it on, through his own right, to his brothers from his father who are not his mother’s sons; for were it not for him, her own relatives would inherit her. And we do not say that he is a stillborn [nefel] and not fit to inherit.
rashi:a18.1: But a fetus: if she died while pregnant, the fetus’s relatives do not inherit her, since it dies first.
rashi:a19.1: And the Gemara answers: this applies, that it dies first, with regard to death, when she dies her own death.
rashi:a20.1: And we object: with regard to [natural] death, does it really die first? But there was an incident, and it moved convulsively after its mother’s death.
rashi:a20.2: The tail of the lizard: if one cuts it off, the cut piece moves convulsively even though there is no life in it.
rashi:a21.1: And one tears open her abdomen: since it sometimes happens that she dies first.
tosafot:a4.1: They raised an objection: one who digs a pit in the public domain: this objects to Rabba, who said above that a loan written in the Torah is not like one written in a document; and so Rabbeinu Tam copied it in his book. It could also have objected to Rav Yosef, since he too holds that a lien is not by Torah law; but [it objects to Rabba because] he spelled out his view more explicitly.
tosafot:a5.1: Rabbi Ila said that Rav said: when he stood trial: Rav did not give this answer because of Rabba’s difficulty, since Rabba lived many years after Rav. Rather, it is because an objection is raised against Rav from this [baraita] in chapter Get Pashut (Bava Batra 175b), where he says that a loan by oral agreement is not collected from the heirs; and he gave the answer for his own view.
tosafot:a6.1: Where the judges sat at the opening of the pit: and even so it was necessary to say “died and buried him,” since you might have thought that we require “Let the owner of the ox come and stand by his ox” (Sanhedrin 19a) [i.e., that the party must be present at the trial]; it teaches us that he properly stood by it.
tosafot:a7.1: They sprinkle for him from the blood of his sin offering and from the blood of his guilt offering: [it names these] since a sin offering and a guilt offering are not sacrificed after the owner’s death, but his burnt offering is sacrificed.
tosafot:a11.1: Sat on the travailing chair, etc.: Rashi explained: before her sentence was concluded. But this is not so, since it refers to one going out to be executed, and every “one going out to be executed” is after the conclusion of the sentence, as is implied in all those cases mentioned above in the mishna in our discussion; and so it is implied in chapter Kol HaGet (Gittin 28b), which speaks of “one going out to be judged” and “one going out to be executed.” And this is the reason of the first clause, that one does not wait, because of affliction of judgment; as is implied in chapter Eḥad Dinei Mamonot (Sanhedrin 35a), that there is affliction of judgment only after the conclusion of the sentence, since it says: How should one act? Let them judge him on Shabbat eve, conclude his sentence on Shabbat and execute him on Sunday? You are then found to afflict his judgment, etc. Let them conclude his sentence on Sunday? They will forget their reasons. [It is concerned there about forgetting,] and about affliction [before the sentence is concluded] we are not concerned.
gershom:a1.1: Rav Yosef said: [they disagree] about a loan, etc.
gershom:a2.1: And it killed him, exempt: the owner of the ox, since [the digger] should not have dug in the public domain.
gershom:a3.1: But if [the ox] died: if the ox died too, the heirs of the owner of the pit are liable to pay. And this is difficult for the one who says that a loan written in the Torah is not like one written in a document.
gershom:a4.1: Rabbi Ila said: actually it is not like one written in a document; but the heirs are liable here because the owner of the pit stood trial and was obligated before he died.
gershom:a5.1: The halakha: [that] the heirs are liable.
gershom:a6.1: But it teaches “killed him” and [the heirs] are liable; [so] he had no time to stand trial.
gershom:a7.1: That it made him: the ox made the owner of the pit a tereifa, and he stood trial and then died.
gershom:a8.1: But doesn’t Rav Ḥagga teach “and buried him”: that the ox buried the owner of the pit by its fall, knocking earth down on him, and both died in that earth and were buried; so it was impossible for him to stand trial. [Rabbeinu Gershom reads “Rav Ḥagga.”]
gershom:a9.1: Actually it is not like one written in a document; so here, why are the heirs liable? For example, where judges sat at the opening of the pit and obligated him immediately, before his soul departed.
gershom:a10.1: They sprinkle for him: on the altar.
gershom:a11.1: From the blood of his sin offering: if he sinned before that and set aside an offering, and afterward his sentence was concluded, they sprinkle for him from the blood of his sin offering before he is executed, so that he gains atonement for that sin.
gershom:a12.1: Sinned at that time: when he goes out to be executed, one does not attend to him so that he gain atonement for that sin.
gershom:a13.1: [Sinned at that time when he goes out to be executed: one does not attend to him, to hold him back until he sets aside his sin offering.] Because one does not afflict his judgment [by waiting] until it is slaughtered and [the blood] sprinkled.
gershom:a14.1: His offering slaughtered: his sin offering.
gershom:a15.1: The woman: a pregnant woman who goes out to be executed. One does not wait for her until she gives birth; rather, one puts her to death with her offspring, since the fetus is like her body.
gershom:a16.1: It is the husband’s property: the offspring.
gershom:a17.1: Until both of them are equal: [both] intentional. [But if one of them was unwitting,] or if she was a minor and he an adult, he is not executed.
gershom:a18.1: That is derived from “also”: when we include the offspring, it is from “also.”
gershom:a19.1: Once it has uprooted: to come out.
gershom:a20.1: So that she not come to disgrace: for if the fetus were alive after its mother’s death, it would move convulsively and come out, and she would stream blood from that place and be disgraced before everyone. Therefore they strike her on the abdomen, opposite the offspring.
gershom:a21.1: A day-old baby: whose mother died when she bore him, and the baby died the next day.
gershom:a22.1: Inherits and bequeaths: he inherits his mother’s property, to bequeath it to his brothers from the father. For if he is from one mother and his brothers from another mother, and he inherited property from his mother, he bequeaths it to the brothers from the father, since paternal brothers inherit one another.
gershom:a23.1: But a fetus, no: that is, where its mother died and it was not born, the brothers do not inherit its mother’s estate, since it dies first in its mother’s womb, before its mother; and a son does not inherit his mother in the grave, having died before her, to bequeath to the brothers from the father. Evidently the fetus dies first; for if she died first, let it inherit her and let the brothers inherit from it.
gershom:a24.1: The drop of the Angel of Death: a drop of gall.
gershom:a25.1: And it made three convulsions: the fetus moved itself three times after its mother died.
gershom:a26.1: That convulsion: it is not a convulsion that has life in it; rather, it is like the lizard’s tail, which moves convulsively after the tail is cut from it.
rashi:b1.1: It is merely cutting flesh: and there is liability [for wounding on Shabbat] only for one who wounds a living creature, drawing blood.
rashi:b5.1: (One may derive benefit from her hair: women whose hair was sparse were accustomed to tie the hair of other women to their own hair, and that is a pe’a nokhrit.)
rashi:b5.3: With a wig: he does not mean her actual hair, but that she had a wig of another woman’s hair tied to her hair [for women whose hair was sparse were accustomed to tie the hair of other women to their own hair, and that is a pe’a nokhrit], and she said: Give it to my daughter. And the mishna teaches us that even though it is tied to her, since she said “Give,” she revealed her mind that she does not want it to be like her body, so as to become forbidden along with it; and it is like something removed during her lifetime.
rashi:b6.1: The hair of righteous women: of an idolatrous city, who were not led astray along with it: what is [the law]? And Rava said there, in chapter Ḥelek (Sanhedrin 112a): he asks about a wig that the righteous woman tied to her hair, whether it is like her body and is saved, or like her property. And we maintain (there) that the righteous within it go out of it naked and all their property is burned, as it is written: “And you shall gather all its spoil,” etc. [Deuteronomy 13:17]. Evidently he is uncertain whether it is like her body or not; so let him resolve it from here that it is her body, since the reason is that she said “Give,” etc.
rashi:b9.1: It is difficult for Rav Naḥman: [namely,] that we explained the mishna as referring to a wig; but it teaches it as similar to an animal, etc. [Rashi’s heading reads “Rav Naḥman.”]
rashi:b10.1: Rather, Rav Naḥman said: actually it is her real hair. And as for your difficulty, that these are forbidden for benefit: it is not difficult, since the hair of a corpse is not forbidden for benefit. It is not like the hair of an animal that was killed, since a woman, her death forbids her, and hair is not subject to death, since it does not change; but an animal, the conclusion of its sentence forbids it, as it says in Pesaḥim, chapter Kol Sha’a (Pesaḥim 22b): From the implication of that which is stated, “The ox shall surely be stoned” [Exodus 21:28], do I not know that it is an unslaughtered carcass and forbidden to be eaten? Why then does the verse state, “And its flesh shall not be eaten”? It tells you that if one slaughtered it after its sentence was concluded, it is forbidden. And I have [derived] only [the prohibition of] eating; from where [do I derive] benefit? etc. Therefore whatever is attached to it at the time the sentence is concluded becomes forbidden with it.
rashi:b11.1: Levi teaches in accordance with Rav: who explains it as where she said “Give,” and as referring to a wig.
rashi:b11.2: Died: and did not say “Give”: one does not give, etc.
rashi:b11.3: A corpse is forbidden for benefit: as it is written: “And Miriam died there” [Numbers 20:1], and one derives “there” from “there” in [the passage of] the heifer whose neck is broken [Deuteronomy 21:4], in tractate Avoda Zara, chapter Ein Ma’amidin (Avoda Zara 29b).
rashi:b12.1: Obvious: that one does not give for this reason, since a corpse is forbidden for benefit. Rather, certainly this is what it is saying: the adornments of the dead, such as a wig, are forbidden for benefit. And that is why it teaches this “because,” since it wants to reveal that it is not dealing with her actual hair.
rashi:b13.1: An animal that was killed is forbidden for benefit: even its hair.
rashi:b15.1: Mishna: One cannot be valuated for less than a sela: for even a poor man, who is judged according to his means, may not give less than a sela.
rashi:b15.2: Nor more than fifty: for that is the largest of the valuations written in the passage.
rashi:b15.3: He gave a sela: [for example,] a twenty-year-old, whose valuation is fifty, was poor and gave a sela for his valuation, since a poor man is judged according to his means; and [then] he became wealthy: he is exempt.
rashi:b15.4: He gives fifty: since with the first giving he did not fulfill [the obligation of] his valuation, and his valuation is still upon him. And a poor man who valuated himself and became wealthy before giving gives the valuation of a wealthy man, as we derive below in chapter HaSeg Yad (Arakhin 17b).
rashi:b16.1: There were five sela in his possession: a poor man of twenty who valuated himself and had five sela.
rashi:b20.1: Gemara: That one comes for all valuations that you valuate: that even the poorest of the poor may not give less. But where he has more, he gives, as it is written: “according to the means.”
rashi:b21.1: The means of the one who vows and not the means of the one vowed: that a poor man who valuated a rich man gives the valuation of a poor man.
rashi:b21.2: Don’t we learn from it by itself, etc.: even though the verse comes for this, “and not the means of the one vowed,” nevertheless “according to the means” is written, and by itself you learn that where his means suffice, take from him.
rashi:b22.1: And he gave four for the second: by the priest’s [assessment], he fulfilled both of them, even according to the Rabbis, since he gave to the second first.
rashi:b23.1: Whatever he has collected he has collected: and therefore when he gives to the first, he gives it all that he has. And regarding the second, one cannot say: Why did he not give all five? Because at the time that he gave to the second, [the money] was liened to the first, so that even what he gave it was not really its own.
tosafot:b16.1: One cannot be valuated for less than a sela, etc.: “Less than a sela and became wealthy” is not specifically less than a sela; rather, even if he gave the entire valuation except for one sela, the whole is imposed upon him.
tosafot:b21.1: That one [comes for] the means of the one who vows and not the means of the one vowed: And if you say: what reason would there be to include the one vowed, that a verse was needed to exclude it? One can say: since the verse is written, “And all your valuations shall be according to the shekel of the Sanctuary” [Leviticus 27:25], [teaching] that a valuation shall not be less than a shekel, and we find a valuation of fifty, one might have thought that this matter, [reducing it] according to means, we know from reasoning, and [then] we would follow the one vowed. [So] the verse teaches us, “according to the means of him that vowed,” that we do not follow the one vowed.
tosafot:b24.1: At the time that he gives to the first, he has nothing: This is puzzling, since at the time that he vowed the first, he had five sela; so how is he exempted when he gave it one? But we learned in chapter HaSeg Yad (below, Arakhin 17b): If he was wealthy, meaning at the time of the vow, and became poor [when he came to pay the priest], or he was poor [when he vowed], gave nothing, and became wealthy, he gives the valuation of a wealthy man. And our teacher says that the mishna below is specifically where the priest assessed him while he was still wealthy, and therefore when he becomes poor he still gives the valuation of a wealthy man; but if he vowed when he was wealthy and was not assessed, and became poor, he gives the valuation of a poor man. And in our discussion this is how it was: he gave four for the second, since the priest assessed him first for the second, and then assessed him again for the first, and according to [the priest’s assessment] he gave one for the first. Therefore he is exempt from it, since he was not assessed for it while the five sela were in his possession.
gershom:b1.1: It is cutting flesh: that is, since she has died, there is no [prohibition of] wounding in her.
gershom:b2.1: An animal that was killed is forbidden for benefit: as we explained from “The owner of the ox shall be clear” [Exodus 21:28].
gershom:b3.1: They are items forbidden for benefit: a corpse, as one derives “there” from “there” from the heifer whose neck is broken.
gershom:b4.1: With a wig: the hair of another woman that was not attached to her hair; and that hair is permitted for benefit.
gershom:b5.1: The hair of righteous women: of an idolatrous city, for we say there that the righteous within it, their bodies escape and their property is lost. And Rava said he asks about a wig: whether it is like property and not her body, or perhaps, since it is attached to her, it is like her body. Certainly, if it is attached to her, he does not ask, since certainly it is like her body and escapes; when he asks, it is where [the wig] is hanging on a peg.
gershom:b6.1: The reason is that she said “Give”: it is like something separated from her.
gershom:b7.1: Just as there, its body: since an animal has no wig, so too here, with a woman, it is speaking of the hair of her body and not of a wig.
gershom:b8.1: Rather, Rav Naḥman said: this is the reason one may derive benefit from her hair: this woman, her death forbids her, for even if she is not executed but dies naturally, she becomes forbidden for benefit. And what it forbids is that which is her actual body, which changes because of death; her hair does not change. Therefore, when she said before her death “Give,” it is like something separated from her, and one may derive benefit from it.
gershom:b10.1: The conclusion of its sentence forbids it: for benefit, and not its death. Therefore, from the time its sentence was concluded, [the sentence applied to all of it,] to its body and to its hair; therefore one may not derive benefit from its hair.
gershom:b11.1: The adornments of the dead are forbidden for benefit: evidently it is dealing with a wig.
gershom:b12.1: And it is taught in accordance with Rav Naḥman, that it is dealing with the actual hair of her body.
gershom:b14.1: One cannot be valuated for less than a sela: one never takes from those who valuate less than a sela, nor more than fifty sela.
gershom:b15.1: [How so? He said: My valuation is upon me, fifty sela, and his means sufficed for only one sela, and he gave it: he is exempt from the valuation, and even if he became wealthy, he gives nothing. But if he gave less than a sela and became wealthy, he gives fifty sela.]
gershom:b16.1: There were five sela in his possession: and his valuation was fifty.
gershom:b17.1: Rabbi Meir says: he gives only one: since his means do not suffice for the whole valuation.
gershom:b18.1: All valuations that you valuate: in general, shall not be less than a shekel; and he is not exempt until he gives a whole sela, as we said above, since it wrote “shekel” for the small valuation and “fifty” for the large valuation.
gershom:b19.1: [Where he has: he gives what he has, as it is written: “according to the means of him that vowed.”
gershom:b20.1: And Rabbi Meir: this “according to the means of him that vowed” comes to exclude the means of the one vowed: that a poor man who valuated a rich man gives a poor man’s valuation, what his means suffice for, and we do not follow the one vowed.]
gershom:b21.1: And don’t [you learn from it, etc.]: that is, you learn both from it: the means of the one who vows and not of the one vowed; and learn from its saying “according to the means” that where his means suffice, we take from him all that he has.
gershom:b22.1: [And he gave four: for the second valuation, and one for the first.
gershom:b23.1: A later creditor: that last valuation is the later creditor who collected first; what he collected he collected. That is, all [five] would have been liened to the first had the second not preceded it; and what the second preceded and collected, it acquired. The one that remained was liened to the first, and at the time he gave one to the first, he fulfilled it, since he had nothing more and his means did not suffice for more. Therefore he fulfilled both of them.]
